title: Bus fare cap (£2 then £3): not expressible, and the reason is specific
registry_rule: A GAP registry. It stages NO value claims — the DfT-commissioned evaluation figures belong to their originators (#86/#91) and are harvested in their own mode-1 lane from primary documents. What is recorded here is the engine gap, the evidence for it, and the upstream change that would close it.

engine_pin.pin_rule: Read from importlib.metadata at write time, never typed as a literal. For a GAP registry the pin matters more than anywhere else: the verdict is only as good as the engine it was searched in. --probe refuses a mismatch.

search_rule: This repo has published two false engine gaps (#100, #101), both from a guessed path that failed to resolve. A gap claim here must be backed by an exhaustive NAME SEARCH. It must search VARIABLES as well as PARAMETERS: the first pass at this measure searched only the parameter tree, concluded bus was absent from the model, and was WRONG — bus_subsidy_spending is a variable and a parameter-only search misses it.

name_search.finding: gov.dft now has three children: bus, rail and spending. The bus node holds ONE parameter, fare_allocation_weight_by_age, and it is not a policy lever — see nearest_levers_and_why_they_do_not_work. There is still no bus fare cap, no bus fare index, and no concession parameter anywhere in the tree.

bus_subsidy_spending.note: Bus subsidy IS in the model as a household-level quantity, and its incidence across households is modelled. So the gap is NOT 'PolicyEngine does not do buses'.

bus_fare_spending.note: Household spending on bus and coach fares (COICOP 7.3.2), CPI-uprated. Consumed by nothing outside a test, so it is a dead-end leaf and not a route to a scoreable outcome.

the_gap: bus_subsidy_spending is a PURE INPUT — no formula, no parameter behind it. Its sibling rail has the price/quantity split that makes a reform possible: rail_subsidy_spending = rail_usage x gov.dft.rail.fare_index. Bus never received it. So the gap is not a missing subject area; it is a missing FACTORISATION. There is no lever to move, which is why a fare cap cannot be expressed even though bus subsidy is present.
upstream_item: Mirror the structure rail already has: a bus_usage quantity, a gov.dft.bus.fare_index parameter, and bus_subsidy_spending = bus_usage x fare_index. Small and well-precedented — the rail side is the working reference implementation. It would make every future fare-cap question scoreable, not only this one.
policy_context: The £2 cap ran through 2024 and was evaluated independently for DfT by Frontier Economics and SYSTRA (final plus interim reports). The £3 cap runs to March 2027, so it is live for the 28 October Budget. The claims are worth holding even while the counterpart is not computable.
contrast_with_rail: #105 is the scoreable half of this pair; the engine ships both legs there.

nearest_levers_and_why_they_do_not_work.description: Raise transport expenses by this percentage.
nearest_levers_and_why_they_do_not_work.why_not: It moves ALL transport expenses by a percentage. It is not bus-specific and it is not a fare cap, so using it would model something other than the measure and label it as the measure.

A container, not a parameter. Its ONLY child is fare_allocation_weight_by_age, ruled out below. It is listed rather than skipped because the existence of a gov.dft.bus namespace is the single most likely thing to make a future reader assume a bus lever exists.

nearest_levers_and_why_they_do_not_work.description: Relative weight used to ALLOCATE a household's bus and coach fare spending across its members by age, derived from National Travel Survey local bus trips and adjusted for concessionary travel.
nearest_levers_and_why_they_do_not_work.appeared_in: 2.92.0 — absent at 2.89.2, when v1 of this registry was written
nearest_levers_and_why_they_do_not_work.why_not: It is a within-household ALLOCATION weight, not a price. It changes who in a household is recorded as bearing the fare spending; it cannot change what a fare costs. A cap is a price instrument, so this node is nearer the subject than anything before it and still not a lever. Notably it also confirms the gap: the engine gained bus DATA structure without gaining a bus POLICY parameter.

corrections_log: v1 was written against 2.89.2 and recorded that gov.dft had exactly two children, rail and spending. At 2.92.0 that is no longer true: gov.dft.bus exists, holding fare_allocation_weight_by_age. The --probe drift check caught this on the first run against the newer engine, which is what it was built for. The VERDICT is unchanged — the new node is an allocation weight, not a price lever, and bus_subsidy_spending still has no formula — but the evidence behind it had gone stale, and a stale gap is exactly what this file exists to prevent.
